about: EC1A1 is the Winter Term microeconomics half unit taken by students on the BSc Economics and BSc Econometrics and Mathematical Economics, after ST109 and EC1P1, with MA100 or MA108 taken before or in the same year. The 2026/27 course guide describes consumer choice under budget constraints and uncertainty (with applications to saving and labour supply), behavioural insights into consumer decisions, firms' decisions across market structures, and the use of theory together with evidence to address policy questions and the role of government. It is distinct from EC1A3, the Autumn Term Microeconomics I course for other programmes, which covers game theory and auctions. Teaching is 20 hours of lectures and 9 hours of classes in Winter Term, 1 hour of classes in Spring Term and 6 hours of online Q&A sessions; formative work includes weekly problem sets, a marked mock exam and a 10-minute policy video presentation. Assessment is a 2-hour exam (plus 15 minutes' reading time) in the Spring exam period worth 85% and continuous assessment worth 15%; there is no set textbook, with Varian and Perloff listed as optional texts.
topics: Policy and the role of government

notes.h: Consumer choice: preferences, budgets and demand
notes.body:
EC1A1 builds consumer theory with calculus, so expect to set up and solve constrained optimisation problems, not just draw diagrams.

Preferences and utility
- Standard assumptions: complete (any two bundles can be ranked), transitive (no cycles), monotone (more is better) and convex (averages are weakly preferred to extremes).
- A utility function u(x, y) represents preferences if it ranks bundles in the same order. Utility is ordinal: any increasing transformation (such as ln u) represents the same preferences.
- Indifference curves join bundles with equal utility. Their slope is −MRS, where MRS = MUx/MUy is the rate at which the consumer will give up y for one more x.

The budget constraint
- px·x + py·y = m. Slope −px/py (the market rate of exchange); intercepts m/px and m/py.
- A price rise pivots the line inwards; an income rise shifts it out in parallel.

Utility maximisation
- Interior optimum: MRS = px/py (tangency) together with the budget constraint.
- Lagrangian: L = u(x, y) + λ(m − px·x − py·y). First-order conditions give MUx/px = MUy/py = λ, so λ is the marginal utility of income.
- Corners: with perfect substitutes (u = ax + by) the consumer buys only the good with higher MU per pound; with perfect complements (u = min{ax, by}) the optimum is at the kink, where ax = by.

Cobb–Douglas example
u = x^(1/3) y^(2/3), m = 90, px = 1, py = 2.
- Cobb–Douglas demands spend fixed shares of income: x* = (1/3)m/px and y* = (2/3)m/py.
- x* = 30 and y* = 30.

Income and substitution effects (Slutsky)
Suppose px rises from 1 to 2.
- New demand: x = (1/3)(90)/2 = 15. Total effect = −15.
- Slutsky compensation keeps the original bundle just affordable: Δm = x·Δpx = 30 × 1 = 30, so compensated income is 120.
- Compensated demand at the new price: (1/3)(120)/2 = 20. Substitution effect = 20 − 30 = −10.
- Income effect = 15 − 20 = −5 (x is normal, so lower real income reduces demand).
- The substitution effect of an own-price rise is always negative or zero. The income effect is negative for normal goods and positive for inferior goods. A Giffen good is an inferior good whose income effect outweighs the substitution effect, so demand rises with price.
- Some courses use the Hicksian version (holding utility, not purchasing power, constant). For small price changes the two give similar answers, so check which your lectures use.

Demand concepts
- Normal good: demand rises with income; inferior: demand falls with income.
- Own-price elasticity ε = (∂x/∂p)(p/x); income elasticity η = (∂x/∂m)(m/x). For Cobb–Douglas, ε = −1 and η = 1.
- Substitutes and complements: the sign of the cross-price effect.

Revealed preference
If bundle A is chosen when B was affordable, A is revealed preferred to B. The weak axiom says B should then never be chosen when A is affordable. This lets choice data test the theory without observing utility.

Exam tips: write the Lagrangian, derive demand in general before plugging in numbers, check corner solutions, and lay out the Slutsky decomposition in three clear steps.

notes.h: Decisions under uncertainty: expected utility and risk
notes.body:
Many economic choices (insurance, investment, education, saving) involve risk. EC1A1 models them with expected utility.

Lotteries and expected value
- A lottery gives outcome wi with probability pi. Its expected value is EV = Σ pi wi.
- A risk-neutral person cares only about EV. Most people are not risk-neutral: they will pay to avoid risk.

Expected utility
- Under the expected utility hypothesis, a lottery is valued at EU = Σ pi u(wi), where u is the Bernoulli (von Neumann–Morgenstern) utility of wealth.
- Unlike consumer utility, u here is cardinal up to positive linear transformations: a + b·u (b > 0) represents the same preferences over lotteries.

Attitudes to risk
- Risk-averse: u concave (u″ < 0), so u(EV) > EU (Jensen's inequality). The person prefers EV for sure to the lottery.
- Risk-neutral: u linear. Risk-loving: u convex.
- Certainty equivalent (CE): the sure amount giving the same utility as the lottery, u(CE) = EU.
- Risk premium = EV − CE: how much expected value the person would give up to remove the risk.
- Arrow–Pratt coefficient of absolute risk aversion: A(w) = −u″(w)/u′(w). For u = √w, A = 1/(2w), which falls as wealth rises.

Worked example
u(w) = √w. A lottery pays 36 or 100 with equal probability.
- EV = 68.
- EU = 0.5 × 6 + 0.5 × 10 = 8.
- CE = 8² = 64.
- Risk premium = 68 − 64 = 4.

Insurance
Wealth 100; with probability 0.25 a loss of 64 leaves 36.
- Without insurance: EU = 0.75 × 10 + 0.25 × 6 = 9, so CE = 81 and EV = 84.
- The actuarially fair premium for full cover equals the expected loss, 0.25 × 64 = 16.
- The maximum premium for full cover makes the person indifferent: 100 − P = 81, so P = 19.
- Any premium between 16 and 19 makes both a risk-averse buyer and a risk-neutral insurer better off: this is the gain from trading risk.
- With a fair premium, a risk-averse person buys full insurance, because it gives 84 for sure, which has higher utility than a lottery with the same EV.

Other applications
- Diversification: spreading wealth over independent risks lowers variance without lowering EV.
- Risk and returns: risk-averse investors require a higher expected return to hold riskier assets.
- Problems in insurance markets: adverse selection (insurers cannot tell high from low risks) and moral hazard (insurance reduces care), which motivate deductibles and, in some markets, compulsory cover.

Limits of expected utility
The Allais paradox (Allais, 1953) shows people often violate the independence axiom that underlies expected utility, for example by overweighting certainty. This motivates prospect theory, covered in the behavioural topic.

Exam tips: compute EV, EU, CE and the risk premium in that order, and when asked about insurance, find both the fair premium and the maximum willingness to pay.

notes.h: Saving and labour supply: consumer theory applied
notes.body:
EC1A1 applies the same choice framework to two big household decisions: how much to save and how much to work. Both are budget-constrained optimisation problems where the "price" is the interest rate or the wage.

Intertemporal choice (two periods)
- Incomes y1, y2; consumption c1, c2; interest rate r.
- Intertemporal budget constraint: c1 + c2/(1 + r) = y1 + y2/(1 + r). Present values must match.
- The price of c1 in terms of c2 is (1 + r).
- Preferences: U = u(c1) + βu(c2), with β the discount factor (impatience).
- Euler equation (interior optimum): u′(c1) = β(1 + r)u′(c2). Give up a pound today, earn (1 + r) tomorrow, valued at βu′(c2).

Worked example
U = ln c1 + ln c2 (β = 1), y1 = 120, y2 = 66, r = 0.1.
- Lifetime wealth W = 120 + 66/1.1 = 180.
- With log utility and β = 1, c1 = W/2 = 90.
- Saving s = 120 − 90 = 30, so c2 = 66 + 1.1 × 30 = 99.
- Euler check: c2/c1 = β(1 + r) = 1.1.

Effect of a rise in r
- Substitution effect: future consumption becomes cheaper, so c1 falls and saving rises.
- Income effect: for a saver, a higher r makes them richer, which raises c1 and lowers saving; for a borrower, it makes them poorer.
- So for a saver the effect on saving is ambiguous; for a borrower both effects reduce c1 (raise saving).
- With log utility, c1 = (y1 + y2/(1 + r))/(1 + β), so a rise in r lowers c1 only through the value of future income.

Labour supply
- Time endowment T split into hours of work h and leisure l = T − h.
- Budget: c = w·h + V = w(T − l) + V, where V is non-labour income. Rearranged: c + w·l = wT + V ("full income").
- The wage is the price (opportunity cost) of leisure. Optimum: MRS between leisure and consumption = w.

Worked example
u = ln c + ln l, T = 24, w = 10, V = 40.
- Equal weights mean half of full income goes to leisure: l = (wT + V)/(2w) = 280/20 = 14.
- Hours h = 10 and consumption c = 140.
- If the wage rises to 20, l = (480 + 40)/40 = 13 and h = 11.
- With V = 0, l = T/2 whatever the wage: the income and substitution effects of a wage change exactly cancel.

Effects of a wage rise
- Substitution effect: leisure is dearer, so hours rise.
- Income effect: the worker is richer, and if leisure is normal, hours fall.
- If the income effect dominates at high wages, labour supply bends backwards.
- Extensive margin: a person works only if the market wage exceeds their reservation wage (their MRS at zero hours). Participation responses are often larger than hours responses.

Policy links
Income taxes cut the net wage; lump-sum benefits raise V and reduce hours through a pure income effect; withdrawal of benefits as earnings rise creates high effective marginal tax rates.

Exam tips: write the budget in "full income" form, solve with the tangency condition, and always split a price change into substitution and income effects with signs explained.

notes.h: Behavioural economics: psychology in consumer decisions
notes.body:
EC1A1 enriches the standard model with insights from psychology. The aim is not to discard rational choice but to model systematic departures from it and to ask what they imply for welfare and policy.

Present bias
- Exponential discounting, U = u(c0) + δu(c1) + δ²u(c2) + …, is time-consistent: plans made today are still optimal tomorrow.
- Quasi-hyperbolic (β–δ) discounting: U = u(c0) + β[δu(c1) + δ²u(c2) + …] with β < 1. All future periods get an extra discount β relative to now. Laibson (1997) used it to model under-saving.
- Example (β = 0.5, δ = 1): a task costs 6 if done on day 1 and 8 if done on day 2.
- Viewed from day 0, both costs lie in the future: 0.5 × 6 = 3 versus 0.5 × 8 = 4, so the person plans to do it on day 1.
- On day 1 the cost of 6 is immediate and the cost of 8 is discounted: 6 versus 4, so they postpone. This preference reversal is time inconsistency.
- Sophisticated agents foresee this and value commitment devices (pension lock-ins, gym contracts, deadlines). Naive agents do not, and keep procrastinating.

Reference dependence and loss aversion
- Prospect theory (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979): outcomes are judged as gains and losses relative to a reference point.
- Loss aversion: losses hurt more than equal gains please; experimental estimates of the loss-aversion coefficient λ are often around 2.
- Diminishing sensitivity: the value function is concave for gains and convex for losses, so people are risk-averse over gains and risk-seeking over losses.
- Probability weighting: small probabilities tend to be overweighted.
- Example (λ = 2, linear otherwise): a 50–50 gamble to win 100 or lose 60 has expected value +20 but prospect value 0.5 × 100 + 0.5 × (−2 × 60) = −10, so it is rejected.
- Endowment effect: people value an item more once they own it (Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler, 1990, with mugs), consistent with loss aversion.

Defaults, inertia and attention
- Defaults matter far more than standard theory predicts. Madrian and Shea (2001) found that automatic enrolment sharply raised participation in a US employer pension plan, with many staying at the default contribution rate.
- The UK introduced workplace pension automatic enrolment from 2012 under the Pensions Act 2008, using the same insight.
- Limited attention: Chetty, Looney and Kroft (2009) showed that posting tax-inclusive prices reduced demand, so consumers under-react to taxes that are not shown on the price tag.

Social preferences
In ultimatum and dictator games, many people give or demand more than pure self-interest predicts, suggesting concern for fairness.

Welfare and policy
- If choices are biased, revealed preference may not reveal welfare. This raises the question of when the government should intervene.
- Nudges (Thaler and Sunstein, 2008) change the choice architecture (defaults, framing, reminders) while keeping all options open.
- Critics worry about paternalism and about which preferences (present or long-run self) should count.

Exam tips: show the β–δ calculation from both dates to demonstrate a reversal, compute prospect values explicitly, and link each bias to a specific policy tool.

notes.h: Firms: costs and decisions across market structures
notes.body:
The producer side of EC1A1 asks how firms choose output and prices, and how the answer depends on market structure.

Technology and costs
- Production function q = f(K, L). Marginal product MPL = ∂f/∂L; MRTS = MPL/MPK.
- Cost minimisation: MRTS = w/r (the isoquant is tangent to the isocost line).
- Example: q = K^0.5 L^0.5, w = 4, r = 1. Tangency gives K/L = w/r = 4, so K = 4L and q = 2L. Then L = q/2, K = 2q and C(q) = 4(q/2) + 2q = 4q: constant returns to scale give constant average and marginal cost of 4.
- Short run: some inputs fixed, so costs split into fixed and variable; average variable cost (AVC), average cost (AC) and marginal cost (MC). MC cuts AVC and AC at their minima.

Perfect competition
- Many price-taking firms, homogeneous product, free entry and exit.
- Profit maximisation: P = MC (on the rising part of MC).
- Short-run shutdown if P < minimum AVC; long-run exit if P < minimum AC.
- Long-run equilibrium with free entry: P = minimum AC and zero economic profit.

Monopoly
- The firm faces the market demand curve, so selling more lowers the price on all units.
- MR = P(1 + 1/ε), where ε < 0 is the price elasticity of demand. Profit maximisation: MR = MC.
- Lerner index: (P − MC)/P = −1/ε. A monopolist always produces where demand is elastic (|ε| > 1), since MR < 0 otherwise.
- Example: P = 100 − Q, MC = 20. MR = 100 − 2Q = 20 gives Q = 40 and P = 60. Profit = 40 × 40 = 1,600. The competitive output would be 80 at P = 20, so deadweight loss = ½ × 40 × 40 = 800. Check: ε = −P/Q = −1.5 at the optimum, and the Lerner index (60 − 20)/60 = 2/3 = 1/1.5.
- Price discrimination: perfect (first-degree) discrimination captures all consumer surplus and produces the efficient quantity; third-degree discrimination charges higher prices in markets with less elastic demand.

Oligopoly
- Cournot (quantity competition): each firm chooses output taking the rival's output as given. With P = 100 − Q and MC = 20, firm 1's profit (80 − q1 − q2)q1 is maximised at q1 = (80 − q2)/2. By symmetry each produces 80/3 ≈ 26.7, so Q ≈ 53.3, P ≈ 46.7 and profit is about 711 each. Output lies between monopoly (40) and competition (80).
- With n identical Cournot firms, total output is 80n/(n + 1), approaching the competitive level as n grows.
- Bertrand (price competition) with identical products and constant MC: price falls to MC even with two firms.
- Stackelberg (sequential quantities): the leader commits first. With these numbers the leader produces 40, the follower 20, and P = 40.
- Collusion: firms could earn monopoly profits jointly by producing 20 each, but each has an incentive to cheat, a prisoners' dilemma that repeated interaction can help sustain.

Exam tips: always write the profit function, differentiate, and solve; state which variable each firm chooses and what it takes as given; compare outcomes against the competitive and monopoly benchmarks.

notes.h: Theory meets evidence: testing microeconomic predictions
notes.body:
A distinctive aim of EC1A1 is to combine consumer and producer theory with evidence. You should be able to say what a model predicts, how one could test it, and what well-known studies found.

From model to testable prediction
- Theory gives signed predictions: demand curves slope down (except Giffen goods), compensated labour supply rises with the wage, a binding minimum wage reduces employment in a competitive labour market.
- Evidence needs a credible comparison: a randomised experiment, or a natural experiment where a policy changes for some people but not others.
- Difference-in-differences compares the change over time in a treated group with the change in a control group, assuming they would otherwise have moved in parallel.
- Elasticities summarise evidence in unit-free form and connect directly to theory (tax incidence, monopoly markups, labour supply responses).

Minimum wages
- Competitive model: a minimum wage above the market wage reduces employment.
- Monopsony model: if an employer faces an upward-sloping labour supply curve, it pays below the marginal revenue product. A minimum wage between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage can raise both the wage and employment, because the marginal cost of labour becomes flat at the minimum.
- Card and Krueger (1994) compared fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, which raised its minimum wage in 1992, with neighbouring Pennsylvania, which did not. Using difference-in-differences they found no evidence that employment fell in New Jersey relative to Pennsylvania. The study sparked a long debate about data and methods.
- For the UK, an independent review of the international evidence for HM Treasury (Dube, 2019) concluded that minimum wages up to the levels studied had caused little loss of employment, while raising the pay of low earners.

Labour supply
- The model predicts that a temporary wage rise should increase hours (intertemporal substitution), since income effects of a one-day rise are tiny.
- Camerer, Babcock, Loewenstein and Thaler (1997) found that New York taxi drivers worked fewer hours on high-wage days, consistent with a daily income target (reference dependence). Later studies questioned how robust this finding is, a good example of how evidence is debated.
- Responses on the extensive margin (whether to work at all) are often larger than responses in hours, especially for second earners and lone parents.

Saving
- Standard theory says the default option in a pension plan should hardly matter, since people can opt out at low cost.
- Evidence on automatic enrolment (Madrian and Shea, 2001) shows defaults have large effects on participation, supporting models with inertia or present bias.

Revealed preference tests
Choice data from experiments or household surveys can be checked against the weak axiom of revealed preference; violations are informative about whether the standard model fits.

How to write about evidence
- State the prediction, the identification strategy (what comparison isolates the cause), the finding and its limits (external validity, measurement, competing explanations).
- Do not overclaim: one study rarely settles a question.

Exam tips: for any policy question, give the competing models, say which empirical design could distinguish them, and cite at most one or two studies accurately.

notes.h: Policy and the role of government
notes.body:
EC1A1 ends by using consumer and producer theory to evaluate policy. The key tools are surplus analysis and the comparison of market outcomes with what is efficient.

Welfare measurement
- Consumer surplus (CS): area under the demand curve and above the price.
- Producer surplus (PS): area above the supply (marginal cost) curve and below the price.
- Total surplus = CS + PS (plus any government revenue, minus external costs).
- With no market failures, a competitive equilibrium maximises total surplus. This is the intuition behind the first welfare theorem: competitive equilibria are Pareto efficient.

Taxes and incidence
- A per-unit tax drives a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive.
- Example: demand P = 100 − Q, supply P = 20 + Q. Equilibrium Q = 40, P = 60.
- A tax of 10 on sellers shifts supply to P = 30 + Q, so Q = 35, buyers pay 65 and sellers receive 55.
- Tax revenue = 10 × 35 = 350. Deadweight loss = ½ × 10 × 5 = 25.
- The economic incidence is the same whether the law places the tax on buyers or sellers. The side with less elastic demand or supply bears more of it (here the slopes are equal, so the burden splits evenly).
- The deadweight loss rises roughly with the square of the tax, so many small taxes beat one large one.

Price controls
A binding price ceiling causes shortages and a deadweight loss; a binding floor causes excess supply. Who gets the scarce good (queues, rationing) also affects welfare.

Externalities
- A negative externality (pollution) means the marginal social cost exceeds the private marginal cost, so the market overproduces.
- A Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external cost at the efficient output corrects this. In the example above, if each unit causes external damage of 10, the efficient output is 35 and a tax of 10 achieves it.
- Coase theorem: with well-defined property rights and low transaction costs, bargaining can reach the efficient outcome whoever holds the rights; in practice transaction costs are often high.
- Alternatives: quantity limits, tradable permits, subsidies for positive externalities.

Public goods
- Non-rival and non-excludable (national defence, basic research). Private markets under-provide them because of free-riding.
- Efficient provision (Samuelson condition): the sum of all individuals' marginal rates of substitution equals the marginal cost.

Market power and information
- Competition policy can limit monopoly deadweight loss; regulation can cap prices.
- Asymmetric information (adverse selection, moral hazard) can justify compulsory insurance or disclosure rules.

Behavioural policy and government failure
- Nudges and defaults (such as pension auto-enrolment) can help people meet their own goals at little cost.
- Government intervention can also fail: information problems, lobbying and unintended consequences. A good answer weighs both market failure and government failure.

Exam tips: draw the diagram, label the areas, compute surplus changes with triangles and rectangles, and state the efficiency criterion you are using.

questions.q: A consumer has utility u = x^(1/3) y^(2/3), income m = 90, and prices px = 1, py = 2. How much x does she buy?
questions.why: Cobb–Douglas demand spends the exponent's share of income on each good: x = (1/3)(90)/1 = 30. The value 45 splits income equally between the goods, ignoring the exponents. The value 60 uses the share 2/3 that belongs to y. The value 15 divides x's spending of 30 by py = 2 instead of px = 1.

questions.q: With u = x^(1/3) y^(2/3) and m = 90, px rises from 1 to 2 (py = 2). Demand for x falls from 30 to 15. What is the Slutsky decomposition?
options: Substitution effect −10, income effect −5
Substitution effect −5, income effect −10
Substitution effect −15, income effect 0
Substitution effect −10, income effect +5
questions.why: Slutsky compensation adds Δm = 30 × 1 = 30, so income becomes 120 and compensated demand is (1/3)(120)/2 = 20. Substitution effect = 20 − 30 = −10 and income effect = 15 − 20 = −5. Substitution −5 with income −10 swaps the two components. Substitution −15 with no income effect attributes the whole fall to relative prices, ignoring that the price rise also makes the consumer poorer. An income effect of +5 has the wrong sign: x is a normal good, so lower real income reduces demand, and the parts must add up to the total change of −15.

questions.q: Using a Lagrangian, derive the demand functions for u(x, y) = x^a y^(1−a) (0 < a < 1) with prices px, py and income m. Show that the share of income spent on x is constant and find the own-price elasticity of demand for x.
markScheme: Sets up L = x^a y^(1−a) + λ(m − px·x − py·y), or uses ln u
First-order conditions lead to MRS = (a/(1−a))(y/x) = px/py
Substitutes into the budget to get x* = a·m/px and y* = (1 − a)·m/py
Expenditure share px·x*/m = a, constant
Own-price elasticity = −1 (and income elasticity 1)
questions.modelAnswer: It is easier to maximise ln u = a ln x + (1 − a) ln y, which represents the same preferences. L = a ln x + (1 − a) ln y + λ(m − px·x − py·y). First-order conditions: a/x = λpx and (1 − a)/y = λpy. Dividing, (a/(1 − a))(y/x) = px/py, i.e. MRS = price ratio, so py·y = ((1 − a)/a)px·x. Substituting into the budget: px·x + ((1 − a)/a)px·x = m, so px·x/a = m and x* = a·m/px; similarly y* = (1 − a)m/py. The share of income spent on x is px·x*/m = a, constant whatever the prices and income. Since x* = a·m·px^(−1), the own-price elasticity is (∂x/∂px)(px/x) = −1, and the income elasticity is 1.

questions.q: A person with u(w) = √w faces a lottery paying 36 or 100 with equal probability. What are the certainty equivalent (CE) and risk premium?
options: CE = 68, risk premium = 0
CE = 8, risk premium = 60
CE = 64, risk premium = −4
CE = 64, risk premium = 4
questions.why: EU = 0.5 × 6 + 0.5 × 10 = 8, so CE = 8² = 64, and the risk premium is EV − CE = 68 − 64 = 4. CE = 68 with no premium treats the person as risk-neutral, but √w is concave. CE = 8 reports the expected utility itself, forgetting to convert it back into wealth by squaring. A premium of −4 subtracts the wrong way (CE − EV); for a risk-averse person the premium is positive.

questions.q: Wealth is 100 and u(w) = √w. With probability 0.25 a loss of 64 occurs. What is the most this person would pay for full insurance?
questions.why: Without insurance EU = 0.75 × 10 + 0.25 × 6 = 9, so CE = 81. Full insurance at premium P gives 100 − P for sure, acceptable while √(100 − P) ≥ 9, so P ≤ 19. The value 16 is the actuarially fair premium (expected loss 0.25 × 64), the minimum a risk-neutral insurer would accept, not the buyer's maximum. The value 3 is the risk premium (EV 84 minus CE 81), which leaves out the expected loss of 16. The value 9 is the expected utility, not an amount of money.

questions.q: Explain, using expected utility theory, why a risk-averse individual offered insurance at an actuarially fair premium will choose full insurance. Illustrate with a diagram or a numerical example.
markScheme: Defines risk aversion as a concave utility function
Defines a fair premium as equal to the expected loss, so full cover gives certain wealth equal to EV
Uses Jensen's inequality: u(EV) > EU of the risky prospect
Notes partial cover leaves some risk at no gain in EV, so full cover is optimal
Gives a correct example (e.g. √w, wealth 100, 25% chance of losing 64: insured utility √84 ≈ 9.17 > 9)
questions.modelAnswer: A risk-averse person has a concave utility of wealth, so by Jensen's inequality the utility of a sure amount equal to a lottery's expected value exceeds the lottery's expected utility: u(EV) > EU. An actuarially fair premium equals the expected loss. With full insurance the person pays this premium and is compensated in full if the loss occurs, so their wealth is the same in both states and equals the expected wealth without insurance. They therefore get u(EV) for certain instead of EU, which is strictly better. Partial insurance would leave some variation in wealth with the same expected value, which is worse for a risk-averse person, so full insurance is optimal. Example: wealth 100, u = √w, a 25% chance of losing 64. Uninsured EU = 0.75 × 10 + 0.25 × 6 = 9. The fair premium is 16, giving 84 for sure and utility √84 ≈ 9.17 > 9.

questions.q: A consumer with U = ln c1 + ln c2 has income 120 now and 66 next period, and can borrow or save at r = 10%. How much does she consume now?
questions.why: Lifetime wealth is 120 + 66/1.1 = 180, and with log utility and no discounting she spends half on each period, so c1 = 90 (saving 30, and c2 = 66 + 33 = 99). The value 93 averages the two incomes, ignoring interest. The value 96.3 compounds future income forward, (120 + 66 × 1.1)/2, instead of discounting it to present value. The value 120 simply consumes current income, ignoring the option to save.

questions.q: A worker has u = ln c + ln l, no non-labour income, and 24 hours to divide between work and leisure. What happens to her hours of work if the wage rises?
options: Hours fall, because she is richer and leisure is a normal good
It cannot be determined without knowing the initial wage
Hours are unchanged, because the income and substitution effects exactly offset
Hours rise, because leisure has become more expensive
questions.why: With equal Cobb–Douglas weights she spends half her full income wT on leisure, so l = wT/(2w) = 12 and h = 12 at any wage: the two effects cancel exactly. 'Hours rise' considers only the substitution effect. 'Hours fall' considers only the income effect. The initial wage does not matter because the demand for leisure here does not depend on w at all when non-labour income is zero.

questions.q: Analyse the effect of a rise in the interest rate on current consumption and saving for (a) a household that is initially a saver and (b) a household that is initially a borrower. Use income and substitution effects.
markScheme: Identifies the price of c1 as (1 + r): a higher r makes current consumption relatively dearer
Substitution effect: c1 falls and saving rises for both households
Saver: income effect is positive (richer), raising c1, so effect on saving ambiguous
Borrower: income effect is negative (poorer), lowering c1, so saving rises unambiguously (borrowing falls)
Notes the budget line pivots around the endowment point (y1, y2)
questions.modelAnswer: In the two-period model the budget constraint c1 + c2/(1 + r) = y1 + y2/(1 + r) pivots around the endowment point (y1, y2) when r changes, becoming steeper. The relative price of current consumption is (1 + r), so a rise in r makes consuming now more expensive in terms of future consumption. The substitution effect therefore reduces c1 and raises saving for any household. (a) A saver lends at the higher rate and is richer: the new budget line lies outside the old one around their chosen point. If c1 is a normal good, this income effect raises c1. The two effects work in opposite directions, so the net effect on saving is ambiguous; with log utility and no future income they exactly cancel. (b) A borrower pays more interest and is poorer, so the income effect also reduces c1. Both effects push c1 down, so borrowing falls (saving rises) unambiguously.

questions.q: A person has β–δ preferences with β = 0.5 and δ = 1. A task costs 6 units of effort if done on day 1 and 8 if done on day 2. What does she plan on day 0, and what does she do on day 1?
options: Plans to do it on day 1, but on day 1 she postpones it to day 2
Plans to postpone to day 2, and does postpone
Plans to do it on day 1, and does it on day 1
Plans to postpone to day 2, but on day 1 does it immediately
questions.why: On day 0 both costs are in the future, so both carry β: 0.5 × 6 = 3 versus 0.5 × 8 = 4, and she plans day 1. On day 1 the cost of 6 is immediate while 8 is still discounted to 4, so she postpones: a preference reversal. Planning to postpone on day 0 comes from applying β only to the later cost, but from day 0 both dates are future dates. Doing it on day 1 as planned would be the time-consistent behaviour of an exponential discounter, ignoring present bias. Planning to postpone but then acting early reverses the direction of present bias, which makes immediate costs loom larger, not smaller.

questions.q: A loss-averse person evaluates gains at face value and losses at twice their size. How does she value a 50–50 gamble to win 100 or lose 60?
options: +20, so she accepts it
+70, so she accepts it
−20, so she rejects it
−10, so she rejects it
questions.why: Prospect value = 0.5 × 100 + 0.5 × (−2 × 60) = 50 − 60 = −10, so she rejects a gamble with positive expected value. +20 is the expected value, ignoring loss aversion. +70 doubles the gain instead of the loss (0.5 × 200 − 0.5 × 60). −20 forgets the probabilities, computing 100 − 120.

questions.q: Explain how present bias can lead to under-saving for retirement and evaluate two policies that might help: automatic enrolment and commitment savings products.
markScheme: Defines present bias using β–δ preferences, with time inconsistency
Explains under-saving: people plan to save 'from next month' but postpone repeatedly (naive agents)
Automatic enrolment: uses inertia so the default is to save; cites evidence (Madrian and Shea 2001; UK auto-enrolment from 2012)
Commitment products: sophisticated agents value restrictions (e.g. Save More Tomorrow or locked accounts), but naive agents may not take them up
Evaluation: preserves choice, low cost; risks of a poorly chosen default rate or illiquidity
questions.modelAnswer: With β–δ preferences (β < 1) a person discounts every future period heavily relative to today, but treats two future periods consistently. Saving involves an immediate cost and a delayed benefit, so from today's standpoint saving 'from next month' looks attractive, yet when next month arrives the cost is immediate and she postpones again. Naive present-biased savers repeat this and accumulate too little for retirement by the standard of their own long-run preferences. Automatic enrolment changes the default so that people save unless they opt out. Inertia then works in favour of saving: Madrian and Shea (2001) found participation in a US plan jumped after automatic enrolment, and the UK introduced workplace auto-enrolment from 2012. It keeps freedom of choice and is cheap, but many people stick at the default contribution rate, which may be too low, so the choice of default matters. Commitment products, such as accounts with withdrawal penalties or plans committing future pay rises to saving (Thaler and Benartzi's Save More Tomorrow), help sophisticated agents who know they are present-biased. Naive agents may not see the need to sign up, and illiquidity can hurt people facing genuine emergencies.

questions.q: A monopolist faces demand P = 100 − Q and has constant marginal cost 20. What price does it set, and what is the deadweight loss?
options: P = 60, deadweight loss 1,600
P = 20 at Q = 40, deadweight loss 800
P = 60, deadweight loss 800
P = 20, deadweight loss 0
questions.why: MR = 100 − 2Q = 20 gives Q = 40 and P = 60. The efficient output is 80, so DWL = ½ × (60 − 20) × (80 − 40) = 800. P = 20 with no deadweight loss is the competitive outcome, where P = MC, not the monopoly. A DWL of 1,600 omits the ½ in the triangle area (it happens to equal the monopolist's profit). P = 20 at Q = 40 finds the right quantity but reads the price off the MC curve instead of the demand curve; at Q = 40 consumers are willing to pay 60.

questions.q: Two identical firms compete in quantities (Cournot) facing P = 100 − Q, each with constant marginal cost 20. What is the equilibrium?
options: Each produces about 26.7 and P ≈ 46.7
Each produces 20 and P = 60
Each produces 40 and P = 20
The leader produces 40, the follower 20, and P = 40
questions.why: Firm 1 maximises (80 − q1 − q2)q1, giving best response q1 = (80 − q2)/2. By symmetry q = 80/3 ≈ 26.7 each, so Q ≈ 53.3 and P ≈ 46.7. Producing 20 each at P = 60 is the collusive (cartel) outcome, which is not an equilibrium of simultaneous quantity choice because each firm would want to expand. Producing 40 each at P = 20 is the competitive or Bertrand outcome. A leader producing 40 and a follower 20 is the Stackelberg outcome, which needs sequential moves, not simultaneous ones.

questions.q: Show that a profit-maximising monopolist sets (P − MC)/P = −1/ε, where ε is the price elasticity of demand. Explain why a monopolist never operates on the inelastic part of the demand curve.
markScheme: Revenue R = P(Q)Q, so MR = P + Q·dP/dQ
Rewrites MR = P(1 + (Q/P)(dP/dQ)) = P(1 + 1/ε)
Sets MR = MC to get P(1 + 1/ε) = MC and rearranges to (P − MC)/P = −1/ε
If |ε| < 1, MR < 0, so cutting output raises revenue and cuts costs
Interprets the Lerner index: markup is larger when demand is less elastic
questions.modelAnswer: Revenue is R(Q) = P(Q)Q, so MR = P + Q(dP/dQ) = P[1 + (Q/P)(dP/dQ)]. Since ε = (dQ/dP)(P/Q), the bracket is 1 + 1/ε, so MR = P(1 + 1/ε). Profit maximisation requires MR = MC, so P(1 + 1/ε) = MC, i.e. P − MC = −P/ε and (P − MC)/P = −1/ε, the Lerner index. Because ε < 0, the markup is positive and is larger when demand is less elastic. If demand were inelastic (−1 < ε < 0), then 1/ε < −1 and MR < 0: reducing output would raise revenue while also lowering cost, so profit could not be at a maximum. A monopolist therefore always sets price where |ε| > 1 (with positive MC).

questions.q: Camerer, Babcock, Loewenstein and Thaler (1997) found that New York taxi drivers worked fewer hours on days when hourly earnings were high. Which model is this most consistent with?
options: Reference-dependent preferences with a daily income target
Standard intertemporal labour supply with substitution towards high-wage days
A large income effect from the high-wage days making drivers richer
A competitive labour demand curve for taxi services
questions.why: Drivers who aim for a daily income target stop early when earnings come quickly, producing a negative relationship between the daily wage and hours. The standard intertemporal model predicts the opposite: a temporary wage rise should make drivers work more that day. An income effect cannot explain it, because one good day barely changes lifetime wealth. Labour demand concerns how many drivers customers want, not how drivers choose their own hours, so it does not explain the finding.

questions.q: Which statement about minimum wages and employment is correct?
options: In a monopsony labour market, a minimum wage set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage can raise employment
In a competitive labour market, any minimum wage raises employment because workers supply more labour
Card and Krueger (1994) found that New Jersey's minimum wage rise caused large job losses relative to Pennsylvania
Theory predicts unambiguously that minimum wages reduce employment in every labour market
questions.why: Under monopsony the firm restricts hiring to hold wages down; a minimum wage in that range makes the marginal cost of labour flat, so the firm hires more. In a competitive market a binding minimum wage raises the quantity supplied but employment is set by the smaller quantity demanded, so employment falls; the second statement confuses supply with employment. Card and Krueger found no evidence of an employment fall in New Jersey relative to Pennsylvania, the opposite of large job losses. The claim that theory is unambiguous ignores the monopsony model, which is exactly why evidence is needed.

questions.q: Explain how the monopsony model of the labour market differs from the competitive model in its prediction about the effect of a minimum wage, and describe an empirical strategy that could distinguish between them.
markScheme: Competitive: binding minimum wage above equilibrium reduces employment (demand falls)
Monopsony: upward-sloping labour supply; marginal cost of labour above the wage; firm hires less and pays less than competitive
Minimum wage between monopsony and competitive wage raises both wage and employment
Empirical strategy: difference-in-differences comparing affected and unaffected areas or groups before and after a rise, assuming parallel trends
Mentions evidence (Card and Krueger 1994; UK reviews finding small employment effects) and limitations
questions.modelAnswer: In a competitive labour market each firm is a wage-taker, and a minimum wage above the equilibrium wage moves employers up their labour demand curve, so employment falls. Under monopsony the employer faces an upward-sloping labour supply curve: to hire one more worker it must raise the wage for all, so the marginal cost of labour exceeds the wage. It hires where marginal revenue product equals this marginal cost, employing fewer workers at a lower wage than in competition. A minimum wage between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage makes the marginal cost of labour equal to the minimum wage up to the supply curve, so the firm hires more, and both pay and employment rise. To distinguish the models, use difference-in-differences: compare employment changes in a region or group where the minimum wage rose (or where it binds more, such as low-wage sectors) with a similar unaffected one, before and after the rise. Card and Krueger (1994) did this for New Jersey and Pennsylvania and found no employment fall, more consistent with monopsony; reviews of UK evidence have also found small effects. The method relies on parallel trends and on the rise being moderate, so very large increases could still reduce jobs.

questions.q: Demand is P = 100 − Q and supply is P = 20 + Q. A tax of 10 per unit is imposed on sellers. Which outcome is correct?
options: Buyers pay 65, sellers receive 55, deadweight loss 25
Buyers pay 70, sellers receive 60, deadweight loss 0
Buyers pay 65, sellers receive 55, deadweight loss 50
Buyers pay 65, sellers receive 55, deadweight loss 350
questions.why: The new supply curve is P = 30 + Q; setting it equal to demand gives Q = 35, so buyers pay 65 and sellers keep 55. Quantity falls by 5, so DWL = ½ × 10 × 5 = 25. Buyers paying 70 assumes sellers pass on the whole tax with no fall in quantity, which only happens with perfectly inelastic demand. A DWL of 50 forgets the ½ in the triangle. A DWL of 350 is the tax revenue (10 × 35), which is a transfer to the government, not a loss.

questions.q: In the same market (demand P = 100 − Q, private supply P = 20 + Q), each unit produced causes external damage of 10. What is the efficient outcome and how can a tax achieve it?
options: Q = 30, achieved by a per-unit tax of 20
Q = 35, achieved by a per-unit tax of 5
Q = 35, achieved by a per-unit tax of 10
Q = 40, because the competitive market is already efficient
questions.why: Marginal social cost is 30 + Q; setting it equal to demand gives Q = 35, and a Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external cost (10) makes firms face the full social cost. Q = 40 is the market outcome, which ignores the externality. Q = 30 with a tax of 20 counts the damage twice, once in the cost curve and again in the tax. A tax of 5 mistakes the incidence split for the size of the tax: buyers and sellers do share the burden, but the tax must equal the full external cost of 10 to reach Q = 35.

questions.q: Explain why the economic incidence of a per-unit tax does not depend on whether the law requires buyers or sellers to pay it, and what determines how the burden is shared.
markScheme: A tax creates a wedge between the buyer price and the seller price equal to the tax
Taxing sellers shifts supply up by t; taxing buyers shifts demand down by t; both give the same quantity, buyer price and seller price
The burden falls more on the side with the less elastic curve
Gives an example or the approximate formula: buyers' share ≈ εS/(εS − εD)
Notes extreme cases: perfectly inelastic demand means buyers bear all
questions.modelAnswer: A per-unit tax t drives a wedge between the price buyers pay (Pb) and the price sellers receive (Ps): Pb − Ps = t. The equilibrium is found where the quantity demanded at Pb equals the quantity supplied at Ps. If sellers pay, the supply curve shifts up by t; if buyers pay, the demand curve shifts down by t. In both cases the same conditions hold, so the quantity, Pb and Ps are identical: who hands the money to the government does not matter. How the burden is shared depends on elasticities. The side that is less able to respond (less elastic) bears more of the tax; approximately, the buyers' share of the tax is εS/(εS − εD), where εD < 0 is the demand elasticity and εS > 0 the supply elasticity. For example, with perfectly inelastic demand buyers bear the whole tax; with demand P = 100 − Q and supply P = 20 + Q (equal slopes), a tax of 10 raises the buyer price by 5 and cuts the seller price by 5.

questions.q:
A worker has preferences u(c, l) = ln c + ln l over consumption c and leisure l. She has T = 24 hours, earns wage w per hour and has non-labour income V. The price of consumption is 1.
(a) Write down the budget constraint in 'full income' form and derive her demand for leisure, her labour supply and her consumption as functions of w and V. [6]
(b) Find her choices when w = 10 and V = 40. [3]
(c) The wage rises to 20. Find her new choices and decompose the change in leisure into a Slutsky substitution effect and an income effect. Explain the signs. [8]
(d) Instead, the government introduces a universal basic income that raises V from 40 to 100, with w = 10. Find the effect on hours and explain it. Briefly discuss whether this is a reason not to introduce such a policy. [8]
markScheme: (a) c + w·l = wT + V; Lagrangian or tangency 1/l ÷ 1/c = w, i.e. c = w·l
(c) New: l = 13, h = 11, c = 260; total Δl = −1
(c) Slutsky full income to afford old bundle at w = 20: 140 + 20 × 14 = 420; compensated l = 420/40 = 10.5; substitution effect −3.5
(c) Income effect +2.5 (from actual full income 520): leisure normal; signs explained
(d) l = (240 + 100)/20 = 17, h = 7: pure income effect lowers hours by 3
(d) Evaluation: no substitution effect from a lump-sum transfer, so efficient relative to means-tested benefits; but funding by taxes lowers net wages; distributional and welfare gains vs hours falls
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Consumption is c = w(T − l) + V, so c + w·l = wT + V: spending on consumption plus the value of leisure equals full income. Maximising ln c + ln l subject to this, the tangency condition is MUl/MUc = (1/l)/(1/c) = c/l = w, so c = w·l. Substituting: w·l + w·l = wT + V, giving l* = (wT + V)/(2w). Hours of work h* = T − l* = T/2 − V/(2w), and c* = w·l* = (wT + V)/2. (If V were so large that h* < 0 she would not work; we assume an interior solution.)

(b) With w = 10, V = 40: full income 280, l* = 280/20 = 14, h* = 10, c* = 140.

(c) With w = 20: full income = 480 + 40 = 520, l = 520/40 = 13, h = 11, c = 260. Total change in leisure = −1.
Slutsky substitution effect: give her just enough full income to afford the old bundle (c = 140, l = 14) at the new wage: 140 + 20 × 14 = 420. Her leisure demand with full income 420 at w = 20 is 420/40 = 10.5. Substitution effect = 10.5 − 14 = −3.5: leisure is now more expensive, so holding purchasing power fixed she takes less of it and works more.
Income effect: her actual full income is 520, not 420, because the wage rise raises the value of her time endowment. Moving from 420 to 520 at w = 20 raises leisure from 10.5 to 13, an income effect of +2.5. Leisure is a normal good, so higher (full) income raises it. Total = −3.5 + 2.5 = −1, so hours rise by 1: the substitution effect dominates here. Note that in labour supply the income effect of a wage rise is positive for leisure (she is a net seller of time), unlike the income effect of a price rise for an ordinary good.

(d) With V = 100 and w = 10: l = (240 + 100)/20 = 17, so h = 7 (down from 10) and c = 170. The wage is unchanged, so there is no substitution effect: this is a pure income effect. She is richer and, since leisure is normal, buys more leisure by working 3 fewer hours.
Whether this argues against a basic income: the fall in hours is a real cost if society values the output or the tax revenue, and a basic income must be paid for, probably through higher taxes that reduce net wages and add substitution effects. However, a lump-sum payment does not distort the marginal return to work, unlike a means-tested benefit withdrawn as earnings rise, which creates high effective marginal tax rates. The fall in hours is also a choice that raises her utility (from ln 140 + ln 14 to ln 170 + ln 17). A full evaluation weighs these welfare gains and redistribution against the cost of financing it and the evidence on how large hours responses are in practice.

questions.q:
Market demand for a good is P = 100 − Q. Production has constant marginal cost 20 and no fixed costs.
(a) Find price, quantity and total surplus if the market is perfectly competitive. [3]
(b) Find the monopoly price, quantity, profit, consumer surplus and deadweight loss. Verify that the Lerner index equals the inverse of the absolute price elasticity at the optimum. [7]
(c) Now suppose two identical firms compete by choosing quantities simultaneously. Derive their best-response functions and the Cournot equilibrium price, quantities and profits. Explain why the firms do not achieve the joint-profit-maximising outcome. [8]
(d) A government wants the monopolist in (b) to produce the efficient quantity. Find the per-unit output subsidy that would achieve this, its cost to taxpayers, and comment on whether this is a good policy compared with alternatives. [7]
markScheme: (a) P = MC = 20, Q = 80, CS = ½ × 80 × 80 = 3,200 = total surplus (PS = 0)
(c) Best response qi = (80 − qj)/2; equilibrium qi = 80/3 ≈ 26.7, Q ≈ 53.3, P ≈ 46.7, profit ≈ 711 each
(c) Joint profit maximised at 20 each, but each firm's best response to 20 is 30: incentive to cheat (prisoners' dilemma); each ignores the price effect on the rival's output
(d) Subsidy s makes MC = 20 − s; efficient Q = 80 needs MR(80) = −60 = 20 − s, so s = 80
(d) Cost 80 × 80 = 6,400; P falls to 20; monopolist's profit becomes 6,400 (the subsidy is a transfer to the firm)
(d) Evaluation: efficient output but large transfer, distortionary taxes to fund it; alternatives: price-cap regulation at P = MC (with fixed costs, average-cost pricing), competition policy, entry
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Under perfect competition P = MC = 20, so Q = 100 − 20 = 80. Consumer surplus = ½ × 80 × (100 − 20) = 3,200; producer surplus is 0 with constant MC, so total surplus is 3,200.

(b) Revenue = (100 − Q)Q, so MR = 100 − 2Q. MR = MC gives Q = 40 and P = 60. Profit = (60 − 20) × 40 = 1,600. CS = ½ × 40 × (100 − 60) = 800. Total surplus = 2,400, so DWL = 3,200 − 2,400 = 800 (also ½ × 40 × 40). Elasticity at the optimum: ε = (dQ/dP)(P/Q) = −1 × 60/40 = −1.5. Lerner index (P − MC)/P = 40/60 = 2/3 = 1/1.5, as required.

(c) Firm i's profit is πi = (100 − qi − qj − 20)qi = (80 − qi − qj)qi. The first-order condition 80 − 2qi − qj = 0 gives the best response qi = (80 − qj)/2. In a symmetric equilibrium qi = qj = q, so q = (80 − q)/2, giving q = 80/3 ≈ 26.7. Total Q = 160/3 ≈ 53.3, P = 100 − 53.3 ≈ 46.7, and each firm earns (46.7 − 20) × 26.7 = 6,400/9 ≈ 711. Joint profit (≈ 1,422) is below the monopoly profit of 1,600, which the firms could share by each producing 20. But that is not an equilibrium: if firm j produces 20, firm i's best response is (80 − 20)/2 = 30. When choosing output each firm counts the fall in price only on its own units, not on its rival's, so it over-expands relative to the joint optimum. This is a prisoners' dilemma; collusion might be sustained only through repeated interaction (and is illegal under competition law).

(d) A per-unit subsidy s lowers the monopolist's effective marginal cost to 20 − s. To produce the efficient Q = 80 it needs MR(80) = 20 − s. MR(80) = 100 − 160 = −60, so 20 − s = −60 and s = 80. At Q = 80 the price is 20 = true MC, so the deadweight loss disappears. But the cost to taxpayers is 80 × 80 = 6,400, and the firm's profit becomes (20 − 20 + 80) × 80 = 6,400: the whole subsidy ends up as monopoly profit. The efficiency gain of 800 must be set against raising 6,400 through taxes that create their own deadweight losses, and the distributional effect of transferring large sums to the firm's owners. Better alternatives may be direct price regulation (a price cap at MC achieves Q = 80 with no subsidy, although with fixed costs the firm would need average-cost pricing or a two-part tariff), competition policy to encourage entry (even a Cournot duopoly raises output from 40 to 53.3), or, if the monopoly is natural, public ownership or regulated access. Regulators, however, face information problems in measuring costs, a form of government failure.
